title: Arrakis report: 76% of enterprise agents sit dormant with live credentials. I build agent governors — here's the finding that worries me most
description: The Arrakis 2026 Autonomous Agents Threat Report reveals that a significant majority of enterprise autonomous agents remain dormant yet retain active credentials, posing security risks. Notably, 76% of agents have not run in 60 days but still have valid credentials and active triggers. Additionally, 24% of dormant agents can be activated externally via unsigned webhooks, and 20% can delegate tasks to other agents with higher permissions, potentially bypassing intended access controls. The report highlights a common operational gap where agent credentials and approvals are not revoked or expired after inactivity, unlike employee access which is promptly removed upon departure.

aiSummary: The report from Arrakis Security, based on telemetry from thousands of production autonomous agents, identifies that 76% of enterprise agents are dormant for over 60 days yet maintain live credentials and active triggers. A substantial portion of these dormant agents (24%) can be externally triggered through unsigned webhooks, creating an attack surface that allows unauthorized activation. Furthermore, 20% of agents have the capability to delegate tasks to other agents with different permissions and receive results beyond their own authorization scope. The CEO of Arrakis emphasizes that while employee access is revoked promptly, dormant agents lack ownership and credential expiration, leading to persistent security exposures. Arrakis offers a behavioral intelligence platform that continuously monitors agent behavior and permissions to detect anomalies and enforce policy adherence.
aiImpact: The persistence of dormant agents with live credentials and active triggers increases the attack surface within enterprise environments. Unsigned webhooks enabling external activation of dormant agents can be exploited to initiate unauthorized actions. The ability of some agents to delegate tasks and obtain results beyond their permission scope can lead to privilege escalation and unauthorized data access. These factors collectively raise the risk of unauthorized access, data leakage, and potential misuse of autonomous agents in production environments.
